# v1.1.0-dev.101: Virtual Windows replace Docking Bays

Pre-release off the `dev` branch. Builds on `v1.1.0-dev.100`.

One large change, and it takes a feature away to do it. Read the last
section before you update if you use Docking Bays.

## A Virtual Window is a real window you dock others into

A Docking Bay was a name and a dashed outline. It grouped windows in the
editor and did nothing at all on your desk. A Virtual Window is an actual
window WLM opens, owns and positions. It has a background, a title bar and
a spot on your screen, and the windows you dock into it sit on top of it.

Move it and they move with it, keeping the spacing you left between them.
Close it and they stay exactly where they were. Nothing you dock is ever
altered, only moved.

There is a new **Virtual Windows** tab beside List and Visual. Create a
container there, give it a name and a monitor, and dock windows into it
from the selection panel in either of the other two views. Its own tab
lists what is inside it and lets you take any of them back out.

## Your layout shows the container, not what is inside it

Dock a window and it leaves the layout. The container takes its place, in
the list, on the canvas and in the profile itself. That is the point of
the feature: one entry standing for five windows, moved and restored as
one thing.

The windows are still saved. They have to be, or there would be nothing to
put back next time. They are just no longer *placed* individually, because
their container places them.

## It never touches the windows you dock

This is worth saying plainly, because the obvious way to build docking is
the wrong one.

Windows can be made real children of another window. It is how the
tabbing tools do it, and it gives you one taskbar button and true
clipping. It also, on every version of Windows since 10 1703, forcibly
resets the DPI awareness of the docked app's entire process, so the app
starts scaling wrongly everywhere and not just inside the container. It
ties that app's message queue to WLM's, so one busy app can freeze the
tray and your hotkeys. And nobody has written down what happens to the
docked window if WLM ever dies without tidying up first.

So WLM does not do it. A docked window keeps its own title bar, its own
taskbar button, its own everything. WLM moves it and nothing more. The
cost is honest: your docked windows still appear separately in alt-tab,
and another app raising itself can land on top of one.

## Showing and hiding the container's title bar

The container's own title bar carries its name, how many windows are in
it, and buttons to hide the bar or close the container. Hide it and the
container is just a backdrop with a small handle in the corner to bring
the bar back. It stays draggable either way.

That toggle only ever affects the container. It never touches the title
bar of anything docked inside it.

## Two limits worth knowing

Docked windows catch up when you let go of the container, not while you
are dragging it. Following per pixel would mean firing a reposition at
every docked app many times a second, which is the kind of thing that
makes other people's apps stutter.

Rearranging your monitors in the Display editor moves windows but does not
yet move containers. Move the container to its new monitor from its own
tab afterwards.

## Docking Bays are gone, and saved bays are not carried over

Bays are removed rather than converted. A profile that had them loads
fine, and the windows that were in a bay are all still there. They come
back as ordinary ungrouped windows, and the bay's name is not kept.

If you have bays you want to keep as Virtual Windows, the honest advice is
to write down which windows were in which before you update, because
afterwards there is nothing left to read it off.

## Install

Auto-updates from dev.53 and later. Otherwise unzip and run.
